But even after my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works had spoken, again these gentlemen have nothing to say, they are playing a waiting game. They were waiting for me, and they are not going to be disappointed. For my part I do not approve of the game they are now attempting to play. When a government has a policy to lay before parliament and the country, it is the duty of that government to state clearly the reasons which actuate it. For my part, Mr. Speaker, 1 am quite ready and intend to utter my opinions on this subject freely and boldly, whatever the consequences may be to my future and to myself. I am going to take a stand on this question, because I believe that the time has come when every man must take a stand upon it. It is not my purpose to play with this question politically; it has been made a football long enough. Fifteen years ago this question was approached by one of the political parties with the sole object of making political capital out of it. I may be pardoned if I look at this question briefly. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Work' has referred to the statute giving existence to the province of Manitoba. He has read a part of the statute, and as it is one of the important bases of my argument, I will recall briefly the facts of the case. The statute giving Manitoba its existence as a province, contained the following clauses:-
Section 22. In and for the said province, the said legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education, subject and1 according to the following provisions:
1.	Nothing in any such law shall prejudicially affect any right or privilege with respect to denominational schools which any class of persons have, by law or practice, in the province at the union.
2.	An appeal shall lie to the Governor General in Council from any act or decision of the legislature of the province, or of any provincial authority, affecting any right or privilege of the Protestant or Roman Catholic minority of the Queen's subjects in relation to education.
3.	In case any such provincial law, as from time to time seems to the Governor General in Council requisite tor the due execution of the provisions of this section, is not made, or in case any decision of the Governor General in Council on any appeal under this section is not duly executed by the proper provincial authority in that behalf, then, and in every such case, and as far only as the circumstances of each case require, the parliament of Canada may make remedial laws for the due execution of the provisions of this section, and of any decision of the Governor General in Council under this section.
It is useless to dwell at any length on the interpretation to be given to the clauses which I have just read. Their sense and meaning have been interpreted by the highest judicial tribunal of the British Empire, the Privy Council in England, and I shall refer to that in a moment. Let me say in passing, that they leave no doubt whatever as to the rights which, under that statute, the minority, either Protestant or Catholic, had to their own schools.
In defiance to that Act, the Greenway government, in 1890, submitted to the Manitoba legislature a Bill which ignored the vested rights which the minority had. This was done for a political purpose, to obtain undue political advantage; however, it 'became the law of the province, and it has remained the law of the province, with slight amendments, ever since. This law might have been disavowed by the federal government. If it had been disavowed, it would probably have been enacted and re-enacted year after year, and it would have kept the province at war wtih the federal government, and a most unsatisfactory state of affairs would have ensued. As the law creating Manitoba contained stipulations providing for a better, more complete and final settlement of the question, in a judicial or ' quasi ' judicial way, it was thought better that the interested parties should have recourse to them.
When the working out of the Manitoba School Act was attempted or rather begun, a number of interested parties questioned the' validity of the law and its constitutionality; this is the case known as the Barrett case. It went from court to court, to the Privy Council in England, and here is the holding of the Privy Council:

Do not misunderstand my intentions, I repeat here that I wish the minority in Manitoba to obtain justice. It is a principle written in letters of gold in the programme of my party, that the rights of the minority must >be respected. . . .
If the people of Canada bring me to power, as I am convinced they will, I will settle this question to the satisfaction of all interested parties. I shall have with me in my government Sir Oliver Mowat, who has always been in Ontario, at the peril of his own popularity, the champion of the Catholic minority and of separate schools. I will put him at the head of a commission, where all the interests at stake shall be represented, and I affirm to yon that I will succeed in satisfying those who are suffering at this moment. Is not Sir Oliver Mowat's name alone a guarantee of the success of this plan?
And finally, if conciliation does not succeed, I shall have to exercise that constitutional recourse which the law furnishes, ' a recourse which I shall exercise completely aud entirely.'
Briefly put, it reads thus: To you Catholics of Quebec, I, your future Prime Minister, promise and undertake that I shall give your people of Manitoba a more complete measure of justice. I will have the great Sir Oliver Mowat with me, he is a friend of the Catholics, always has been.
This speech inflamed Catholic enthusiasm in Quebec, and the small fry, the ward-heelers, went with that speech throughout the province, adding on to it special comments, such as the following which I had heard at almost every meeting during that election, and which ran thus:	Now gentlemen, you see what this
great man Laurier will do for his Catholic people in Quebec. Do you not think that Catholic Laurier will do better than Protestant Tupper?
That's what Sir Charles Tupper said in Winnipeg, reversed.
My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) instead of attempting to deny this admits it and tries to bring in Sir Charles Tupper, which is entirely beside the question.
What did you say?

What I said then I am saying now. I would suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that they take their 1 medicine like men. We are told, and it is

true, that a great many of our own people went back on Sir Charles Tupper, and did not extend to him the ' glad hand ' of gratitude.
I am not here to approve of what they did. To say the least, I think they made a great mistake, but it is, to a certain extent, explained by the fact that when appeals are made to religious enthusiasm, either Catholic or Protestant, we always find people who allow themselves to be carried away by them.
Like the navy question in Quebec last election.

We will let the navy rest for the moment with the remark that a gentleman who has been -a judge ought to know that we should try each question judicially. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) were addressing a jury no doubt he would speak about the state of the weather outside the courthouse. But let him come with me to Massey Ha'll, Toronto, and hear what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said there, and I quote from the Toronto ' Globe ' so that there be no mistake about it.
Mr. Laurier said: He was there (in Toronto) to say, not that he would give either a small or a large amount of relief to the minority, but that assisted by his friend, Sir Oliver Mowat, he would settle the question, not by appeal to any class, but by appeal to the sense of justice which was emplanted in every one by the Creator . . . He was a Roman Catholic and a French-Canadian, and, therefore, might have strong sympathy for the minority, but as he himself would not be coerced by anybody, so he would not consent to force coercion upon any one.
This is the same man who said in Quebec, that he would give a big measure of relief. In Massey hall he would not say whether it would he big or a small measure. At first sight there are many words in the Toronto speech which resemble the Quebec one, but mark the ending. The cry in Ontario had been * do not coerce Manitoba/ and we find on the lips of the Laurier of that time, the very same words, put there, no doubt, for a purpose. There was enough in that speech to allow the Griit press and the Grit speakers to go about and say all over the province: 'Look at the great man we have as our future Prime Minister, he will not coerce Manitoba.' The Grit candidates went upon the hustings with the Remedial Bill in their hands and said: ' If we are returned to power, we will take that Remedial Bill and tear it to pieces, shouting: ' Hands off Manitoba.'
Nothing the matter with that.

I am not surprised at that. This is the same double-faced policy Mr. PELLETIER.
we have had for fifteen years. What, Sir, was the result of all this? Quebec sent a majority to put in power the man who promised to give a better measure of justice to the Catholic minority of Manitoba, and the English-speaking Protestants Sent a majority to bring to power the man who would not coerce Manitoba. Meanwhile, the Manitoba minority lay by the way-side knowing full well what they could expect from the government which the leader of the opposition did not wish to coerce.
A commission had been promised which would look into the question and solve it; instead of that, there was a conference between the Manitoba Grits and the Ottawa Grits, where sunny smiles and sunny ways, we were told, would produce important results.
What those results were, I need not mention. except to say, in a word, that, during fifteen long years, a great number of Roman Catholics in Manitoba have been obliged to pay for the maintenance of schools which their children did not attend, and have had to put their hands in their pockets a second time, to have other schools where, according to their belief, they could send their children for their education. Then we heard, falling from the lips of His Majesty's representative in this country, the Governor General, the following words, which were pronounced at the opening of parliament in 1897:
Immediately after the last election, the government of Manitoba was invited to hold a conference' with my ministers on the subject of the grievances arising out of the Act of that province relating to education. Three members of the Manitoba government came to Ottawa, and, after many and protracted discussions, a settlement was reached between the two governments, which was the best arrangement obtainable under the existing conditions of this disturbing question. I confidently hope that this settlement will put an end to this agitation which has marred the harmony and impeded the development of our country, and will prove the beginning of a new era to be characterized by generous treatment of one another, mutual concessions and reciprocal good-will.
Later, the question was asked by Mr. LaRiviere, now a .senator, who was then a member of this House, and reply was given by the then Prime Minister, who is now the leader of the opposition. Let me quote that also:
Mr. LaRIVIERE asked:
By whom was the settlement of the school question signed, after the same was agreed upon by both the federal and provincial governments, and why are not the names given in the copy brought down?
The PRIME MINISTER (Mr. Laurier.) I have alrealy stated to the honourable gentleman that the negotiations -which took place between the Canadian and the Manitoba government were confidential. When they were

concluded, the terms of the agreement were communicated to the press and taken back to Manitoba by the commissioners of the Manitoba government, and afterwards embodied in the Act of the legislature.
However, it was discovered later that the agreement which was brought down without any signature, contained two signatures -those of Wilfrid Laurier and Thomas Greenway.
Before closing what I may call the historical part of my remarks, I wish, once again, in the year 1912, to put on ' Hansard ' something which was said in this parliament when the Liberal government came into power. Sir Charles Tunner, the man who went to the election, with his government, to have a judgment of the Privy Council and the constitution of this country upheld, who was defeated in that manly, courageous, and righteous attempt, stood up in the House, and spoke thus:
In the future, as in the past, the cardinal principle of the party to which I belong, will be:	Equal justice to all, without respect to race or creed. I am glad to know that the responsibility of settling this question-an important question-I am glad to know that the responsibility no longer rests upon my shoulders, but upon those of the honourable gentleman who is now the First Minister of the Crown. I can only say that I trust and hope that he will be most succes-ful in obtaining such a settlement _ of this question as will do justice and give satisfaction to al'l parties. I can assure the honourable gentleman not only that he ha9 my most cordial wishes for a happy, and early, and fair settlement of this important question, hut that anything I can contribute to that end will be at all times most cheerfully done.
A most noble and patriotic move, which has not, I think, its parallel in the history of this country. These words were uttered at a moment when the new leader of the new government, (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) could do alone what he had promised to Quebec, but, for fear that he might be handicapped in some way, this great statesman, who had just fallen in the accomplishment of his duty, turns to the man who had1 profited by the sacrifice, and tells him: "I will not do as you have done, on the contrary, I will help you for the sake of the cause."
I hope the right hon. leader of the opposition will not be offended if I now put him and Sir Charles Tupper side by side, and ask this country to make a comparison between the two. The comparison will be made anyway in the history of this country, and we may as well have it now.
You have now, Mr. Speaker, the facts of the past; they had to be stated in order to show the present state of affairs. These facts are so closely connected with the consideration of what we are told should have been inserted in this Bill now before us
that they must be recalled in order to thoroughly understand the position which I take in, this matter.
It is now suggested that this battle be' fought over again, in respect to the district of Keewatin. If it has to be, in the first place I may say, and say emphatically, with due respect and deference, that there are two things about which I am sure and about which I will not have one moment of hesitation. With my experience of the past, I am not prepared to leave the rights of any minority, either Protestant or Catholic, to the tender mercies of the leader of the opposition and his friends. I would rather leave them in the hands of the Rob-lin government. If future facts show that in doing this I have erred, I will stand the consequences. I am prepared to do so because I believe from the bottom of my heart that I am right. I shall have to again refer to that later.
Has my hon. friend any understanding with the Roblin government?

That is too thin. I am going to answer the question fully by and bye. The Minister of Public Works has answered it and what the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) wants is to enable the Toronto 'Globe' to-morrow to say: Roblin has purchased the consent of the Roman Catholic members of the government. He will not have that chance.
I do not want it. All I want my hon. friend to do is to tell me the truth.

You are going to have the whole truth. The other thing about which I am sure is that it would be most unjust to tell us here to-day that we will be just as bad as the leader of the opposition if we do not give the people of Keewatin more than he gave the people of Manitoba. In the first place, the cases are not alike, and moreover the settlement of the Manitoba school question on just and fair terms was a very easy thing in 1897. The then leader of the government was not only pledged to it, but the opposition offered to help in the settlement, but the present leader of the opposition refused to do anything fair and reasonable.
He decided not to fulfil the promises contained in his Quebec speech, but to stand by his Massey Hall ' no coercion ' programme, and to educate the people of this country on those lines. For the last fifteen years, this has been considered by the people of this country as a good and sound policy. The law of the land has been put to one side, dhe to that attitude of the leader of the then government and his party. The very constitution has been trampled under foot. A remedial order,

which the Privy Council has declared to be a valid and legal remedy, was ignored, and the Liberal party of this country is responsible for all this. Now, I am not here to say that this should be forever continued', and that this should endure forever. I would say: let us put an end to it now and come back to the sane and sound principles which obtained in the past, and which are the safeguard of every citizen of this country, but in the name of the most elementary principles of justice and fair-play. I ask those two questions: If there is to-day within easy reach, a possible way of settling this vexed question should we, in the first place, He asked to uselessly run upstream against the torrent which the Liberal party has set running from the mountain; should we give a chance to the Liberal party to set this eomtry ablaze a second time with one appeal to Quebec and another appeal to Ontario? 'Shall we thereby take upon ourselves the responsibility of asking our political friends to go down to defeat once more to the detriment of the minority, and for the benefit of those who have ignored1 it yesterday, and who would, to-morrow, continue that same policy?
Again, I say that if the purpose in view can be obtained in some other ways, this would be nonsensical and suicidal. I am not prepared to help the gentlemen opposite to continue their policy of setting race against race, and creed against creed in this country. Why, Sir, where would this end? Yes, where would it end? I put this question here as a good1 Canadian. I have been told that I must resign, that there must be a big crisis. Well, Sir, let me tell these gentlemen who speak thus, that there is not enough in that portfolio for a man to forget his honour and his principles, and were it not that 1 consider I have here a noble duty to perform, it is not one, nor ten portfolios winch would make me stand the torrent of abuse, organized and unorganized, which is showered upon me. There has been created, during the last fifteeen years, a certain state of public opinion, people have been educated to believe that, year in and year out, what is right shall be ignored, and what is wrong will triumph and that minorities have no rights. And when a part of the public mind has been so moulded during so many years, I am asked to undo all that in a few months, nay, in a few weeks. A certain part of the public mind misled by the men in power, and their newspapers has, in some respects, to be recast, and a new definition has to be made of what, in certain respects, is right or wrong, and it it the duty of the successors of the Fathers of Confederation to do it. Why, Sir, the Grit newspapers of this country will lie to raise a race cry about the name of a Mr. PELLETIER.
country post office. They will say that Bourassa has ordered the change, and they will organize indignation meetings. Other men will have the audacity to ask me to decide questions in a certain way, not because it is right, but because this or that man is a Catholic or an Orangeman! For the last four weeks the Grit press of Ontario shout that Borden will yield to Bourassa, and impose separate schools in Keewatin, and the Quebec Grit press say wi are going to betray the Catholics by not having separate schools.
Now, can this be? . And will it be tolerated by the people much longer? As I understand it, one of the noble aims of this government is to try and bring all the people of this great country together; to make Canadians love one another more and to make the people understand that if you are a Christian, one of the very first of the Christian principles tell you not to do unto others what you would not like done unto you. I am here to try and help in this most noble work. If 1 have to suffer for that, I will, and am prepared for it; but I am not going to be ' stampeded 5 by a temporary outburst of public opinion which should not exist and which I believe is most unfortunate. With my back to the wall, I shall face it like a man, and wait for better days and a more sober judgment.
Some very good people are very much concerned about the people in Keewatin. So am I, but it is a fact-is it not?-that what is involved in Keewatin at the present moment is a large area of territory with almost no population. I am more concerned about the people who are alive who are up and doing in Manitoba. There were two courses open to me; I might have gone and told Manitoba: * You will remain the postage-stam.p province of this country for all time, if you do not consent to have for Keewatin, school laws as I want them.' This is one course. What is the other? It is to expect from the people of Mani-toa themselves that the Catholics of that province, both for Manitoba and Keewatin, will not pay a double tax if they want to have their children educated as their conscience dictates.
The first of those two courses resembles somewhat what the Catholics tried in 1896, but it had a lamentable fate, because politics interfered in a question which ought to have been put on a higher plane and advocated from a broader point of view.
At that time, as I said a moment ago, the battle could have been won, and won easily. Up to that moment, the great political men of both political parties when enacting laws, had been mindful of the rights of minorities, and it was a very easy thing to have clauses put in any statute, protecting those rights. The fathers of

confederation put it in the British North America Act, and a long series of statutes have been adopted on the same lines.
The statute of 1875 relates to the terri

tories. There you find the same thing enacted in a law, at the request of a Liberal government, but of a government in which were such men as Edward Blake (who has just been called to his reward, and who was a great Canadian). However, all this came to naught and became a perfect wreck, when the people of this country were told that the pact of confederation could be ignored for the purpose of putting a certain political party into power. The people of this country know now that the government of a province can, in defiance of the clear terms of the constitution, enact a law which will do away with the very basis of that constitution, and the people of this country know now that this hitherto inconceivable attempt will be successful, if, thereby, a political advantage can be obtained. In view of all this, if the minority can be otherwise protected, the attempt to force educational laws on Manitoba does not appeal to me as being the best course to follow.
The other course is to expect that the men in power in Manitoba, who are the successors of the fathers of confederation, who have been the friends of the minority over there, will settle this matter once and for all, at home, as they have the power of doing.
How are they going to do that, will the hon. minister tell us?

How sorry the hon. member (Mr. Macdonald, Pictou) would be if this question were taken once for all out of politics, and if he no more had the op' portunity to raise cries of race and creed. But I will come back to the point later.
There is another important point to which I want to refer now. I said a few moments ago that I was more concerned with Manitoba than with Keewatin, because the needs of Manitoba are far greater and much more pressing than those of Keewatin. Let me now state the fact that I have made a careful study of the different problems which have arisen, and one of them, the most important, to my mind, is whether the school rights of the Manitoba minority which have been given away by the late government, can to-day be restored by this parliament? Let us look into the facts: Those rights unquestionably existed; the Privy Council has said so; and there is, consequently, no possible doubt in that respect; it cannot, be denied that they have been put aside.
There is no doubt that they could have been restored in a certain way, provided
for by the constitution; this is also undeniable, because, again, the Privy Council has so declared. The way they could have been restored was by an appeal such as the one which was made. Such an appeal was made, and it is precisely at this moment that the question goes through an interesting phase. The appeal was by the minority to the Governor General in Council, and it was then ' lis pendens ' between two welj-lknown parties; one of them, the appellant, was that same minority, and the other party, the respondent in the case, was the provincial government; the justices were the ministers of the Crown here. They were so to speak, constituted a court of justice to hear that appeal. The appeal was heard and decided in a certain way, and the constitution did not allow of an appeal from their decision, which was a final one. The ordinary courts of this country and every country have been invested with power to see that their judgments are executed and obeyed, but, in this special case, the law gave the Governor General in Council the right to decide in a certain way and the law went just a little further and said: ' When you have decided you will issue an order to the province ' which has lost its case, and there your powers will end.'
It is presumed that the men who enacted that law fully expected that that judgment or order would be obeyed, that there was a moral certainty that it would be; judging from a high sense of justice, they probably had reason to expect that a government would not set at defiance the judgment so rendered. However, the Manitoba government took upon itself this responsibility. What next? Did not the Governor General in Council become ' functus officio ' when the judgment or order was rendered and served upon the province of Manitoba? If so, that case, in which the litigants were the minority on the one side and the provincial government on the other, became a thing of the past, and the power of the Governor General in Council ceased. Another remedy was then provided for, but this remedy was no longer in the hands of the Ministers of the Crown alone, and it could be used only if the majority of the members of both Houses of parliament- were in favour of it. This was the remedial legislation, and when it came to remedial legislation, the parties in the case were the government of Manitoba on the one side, and the members of the government of Canada on the other; and parliament, was the judge, as the King's advisers in this country, the government submitted a Bill to implement the legislation which Manitoba refused to enact. The remedial order had been disobeyed, this remedial legislation had fallen through when the new government which was, constitutional-

ly speaking, the continuance of the preceding government, came into power in 1896. They could have done either of the two following things: Ask parliament to enact remedial legislation, or, by persuasion or otherwise, induce the Manitoba government to obey the remedial order, they had it in their power to do so, they were the only men, or body of men who could do so. What did they do? They decided that remedial legislation was not the proper thing. They thought they would sit down and settle this question by obtaining a partial acquiescence from the Manitoba government to the remedial order, and they decided to abandon the other part of that remedial order and throw it to the winds. Those are hard, historical facts. Can it be pretended at this moment that this settlement, unfair and inadequate as it is, can be legally and constitutionally set aside? Let us look at the way in which it was arranged. Members of the Dominion government called to their office the members of the provincial government; there, we have face to face the people who, constitutionally, issued the remedial order, and the people who disobeyed it.
There they make a hard and fast bargain which the Manitoba legislature put into the form of a statute, and of which the Governor General of Canada, speaking from the Throne in parliament says: * This question is now settled forever. Both Houses of Parliament assent to that.' The question I might now ask is: is it final or is it not final ? I am not going to say that it is or that it is not. I am not going to admit that it is final, because I do not wish to prejudice the case or anything which might crop up in future. I shall remember that I am one of the men who govern this country for a time; that I, like other men, will, some day or other, be called elsewhere as God will decide, and I shall not say anything which might prejudice any future claim, but I am bound to go so far as to say that this right of appeal, this remedial legislation which was a very easy weapon at hand in 1896, has now become much more involved and much more difficult of access.

My hon. friend (Mr. Proulx) was about to make a speech when the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk) rose, and now he has swallowed his contemplated speech. But there are other reasons which give us a right to hope in the justice of a good government. I understand that there are a certain number of public men in the province of Quebec and elsewhere who have taken the stand that the Catholics in Keewatin have certain vested rights in separate schools, and that this Bill ought to contain a clause making it clear that those rights shall continue to exist.
Now I am not resting my case only on hope for relief from Manitoba. There are other reasons which, it seems to me, make this, by far, the best course. I understand that a certain number of important public men from the province of Quebec and elsewhere, have taken the stand that there are vested rights in favour of separate schools in Keewatin, and that those rights would be thrown to the winds if this Bill did not contain a clause, making it clear that these rights shall continue to exist. Let us face

the situation squarely and let us meet it unhesitatingly. Are there such vested rights in Keewatin now? I may say that I have looked into this question with a great deal of care, I have read all the legislation on the subject, and I am bound to say that at a given moment I found a very strange state of affairs. The Northwest Territory Act, passed in 1875, provides for separate schools, but that statute excludes Keewatin from its operations. Moreover, this law of 1875 did not come into force until 1876, by proclamation of the Governor General in Council and before this Bill of 1875 came into force, there was another Bill passed by this parliament in 1876, containing all the enactments which the parliament of that time thought necessary for Keewatin. Whilst the Bill of 1875 contained a clause about separate schools the Keewatin Bill contained no such clause. If you read the debate in * Hansard ' of 1876 about this you will see that the Hon. Mr. Mackenzie, then Prime Minister, declared that this was no oversight. Hon. L. R. Masson, one of the important members of parliament at that time, put the question to him. His answer was: It is not necessary to provide for education in Keewatin. I am not going to discuss whether his reasons were good or bad, I simply refer to Mr. MacKenzie's words to show that I made no mistake in declaring that there was no provision for separate schools in the Keewatin Act.
It is useless for me to dwell at any length on the consequences of that statute, because something else occurred. That Keewatin statute disappeared from what is admittedly the law of the country, viz.: The Revised Statutes of 1906. The manner in which it was done is indeed very strange. The Keewatin Act was never repealed by any special statute, it contained a clause which reads as follows:-
Provided always, that the Governor in Council may, by proclamation published in the ' Canada Gazette,' at any time when it appears in the public interest to do so, detach any portion of the said district therefrom and re-annex it to that part of the Northwest Territories of Canada not included in the said district, and the portion so detached shall then be subject to the same government and laws as that part of the Northwest Territories of Canada to which it is re-annexed.
It is to be noted that this clause gave the Governor General in Council the power, when it appeared to be in the public interest, to detach a portion from another portion of Keewatin. It is quite clear t-hat this clause never gave the power to annex the whole of Keewatin. In the year 1905, the then government had a Bill before this House, dealing with Keewatin, and providing that it should be part of the Northwest Territories. At that time, there
was a good deal of discussion and trouble about the Alberta and Saskatchewan Bills, and it is a fact of public notoriety that certain members of the government of that day were not great friends and that there were serious rows around the council table over the famous clause 16. At a given moment, the Keewatin Bill, which would' probably also have caused trouble, was withdrawn, and four days after the session had closed, that same government, which had withdrawn the Bill, and had told parliament that it was not necessary to deal with the situation in Keewatin, passed an order in council in which they formally said: We have, under the law, a right to detach from Keewatin some portion of it and in virtue of the power so given to us to divide Keewatin into two portions and annex one portion to the territories; we, the government, declare that we annex to the territories the whole of Keewatin. Here is the text of the order in council, as it appeared in the ' Canada Gazette ':
Whereas, in and by the Act, chapter 53, of the Revised Statutes of Canada, commonly known as the Keewatin Act, amongst other things, in effect enacted, that our Governor in Council may at any time when it appears to the public advantage so to do, detach ' any portion ' of the district of Keewatin ' therefrom ' and re-annex it to that part of the Northwest Territories of Canada not included in the said district, and that portion so detached shall become subject to the same government and laws as that part of the Northwest Territories of Canada to which it is re-annexed;
And whereas it has become expedient that the said district of Keewatin should he again annexed to and made subject to the same government and laws as the Northwest Territories;	_

Of all which our loving subjects and all others whom these presents concern, are hereby 'required to take notice and govern themselves accordingly.

I deem it my duty to let the House know the position I took upon the vote this afternoon on the amendment to the Bill proposed by the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I did not vote on that amendment for the following reasons: The Bill now before the House is an Act to provide for the extension of the boundaries of Manitoba.	,
This Bill has its financial aspect and its religious aspect. So far as its financial aspect is concerned I have every reason to believe, so far as my information goes, that both political parties have agreed, except so far as immaterial matters are concerned. But when I heard the leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) state, in moving his amendment that, so far as the religious question was concerned, he would stay within the lines of ' Torres Vedras,' I thought I had better wait a little and see whether there was a very strong position in ' Torres Vedras ' or not. I claim that the leader of the opposition has no right, after putting such an amendment as this before the House, to take the stand he took this afternoon. That is the reason I did not vote on the amendment because the financial aspect of the Bill is not directly under discussion now. It may be discussed when the Bill is considered clause by clause in committee. But now we are dealing with the principle of the Bill on the second reading. And I accept the authority of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk), under whom at Laval I once studied the constitutional law of this country, and it has not been proven to me by the speeches so far made that there is such Federal authority in this House as has been contended. We may not agree absolutely upon the special conditions put in the Bill, but now we are called upon to vote on the principle of the measure which provides for the extension of the boundaries of Manitoba. And I state plainly here that I have no objection to the boundaries of Manitoba being extended. So I am proud to support the present government. Being a new member of this Mr. PELLETIER.
House, I was rather disposed to favour the amendment, if I could have found in that amendment elements of truth, faithfulness and a real desire to serve the minority in Keewatin. But seeing in it a double-faced policy in a djouble-faced amendment, I could not vote for it.
I wish to be very brief in my remarks, but to give my own statement of the position taken by the Postmaster General. I have some information in regard to the matter. In 1878, the Conservatives brought before the country the National Policy. In 1882, in 1887 and in 1891 they appealed to the people on that policy. And what was the policy of the Liberal party? It was a changing, an indefinite policy. But when it came to the election of 1896, the Liberals were in favour of a policy of reciprocity, but the Conservatives still stood before the people on the National Policy. The Liberals came into power with the present leader of the opposition at their head, but he knew, as everybody knew, that he had not the support of the country on his tariff policy. So, he stood by the National Policy, because he knew that elections were won for his party on a double-faced policy on the Remedial Bill. This was understood1 plainly in this House and in the country. So elections were carried by his party with one policy for Quebec and another for Ontario -a policy stated in Jacques Cartier hall for Quebec, and in Massey hall for Ontario. But favouring a policy of protection, they carried the elections of 1900, 1904 and 1908. And in 1911 they came before the country again on a policy of reciprocity. I state without fear of successful contradiction that for the last twenty years the public vote of Canada has pronounced unquestionably in favour of the protective tariff.
Now, all this may seem to be a digression. But it is only to show that behind the walls of Torres Vedras there is a man who is not sincere and who wishes to play a double game.
